title: Pious Fraud in Antiquity
description: Writing in another's name, from Daniel to the disputed letters of Paul, and two letters about Jesus that no one in his time wrote

concepts.title: Pseudepigraphy and Its Ancient Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Pseudepigraphy (from Greek pseudepigrapha, "falsely ascribed") means a text circulating under the name of someone who did not write it. Followers of Pythagoras credited their own treatises to the master, and Iamblichus (c. 245 to c. 325 CE) praised them for rarely claiming credit. Jewish writers of the Second Temple period wrote in the names of ancient worthies. The Book of Daniel, set at the Babylonian court in the 6th century BCE, is dated by most scholars to about 167 to 164 BCE, during the Maccabean crisis. The oldest parts of 1 Enoch, written in the name of the patriarch Enoch, are earlier still.

The physician Galen (129 to c. 216 CE) saw a scroll labeled "Galen the doctor" rejected in a Roman bookshop because its style was wrong, and he went on to write a guide to his genuine works. Tertullian, writing about 200 CE, reports that a presbyter in Asia Minor who composed the Acts of Paul confessed he had done it "out of love for Paul" and was removed from office. The Muratorian Fragment, an early list of accepted books (usually dated to the late 2nd century, by some to the 4th), rejects letters "to the Laodiceans" and "to the Alexandrians" as forged in Paul's name.

The modern label "pious fraud" (Latin pia fraus) names the idea that a deception can serve a holy end. Whether ancient pseudepigraphers saw themselves that way is an open question. In the 5th century the priest Salvian of Marseilles published a treatise under the name "Timothy"; found out, he told Bishop Salonius that readers would have ignored it had they known it came from an obscure author like himself.

concepts.title: Forged Letters in the New Testament?
concepts.contentHtml:
The New Testament contains thirteen letters bearing Paul's name. Critical scholars broadly agree that seven are his, namely Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Doubts about the others turn on style, vocabulary and theology. A large majority of critical scholars judge the Pastoral letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) not to be Paul's. Ephesians is widely doubted, and opinion is more evenly split on Colossians and 2 Thessalonians. 2 Peter, which seems to know a collection of Paul's letters (2 Peter 3:15 to 16), is the letter most widely judged pseudonymous. The Gospels are another matter, since they are anonymous and their authors' names were attached later.

In Forged (2011) and its academic counterpart Forgery and Counterforgery (2013), Bart Ehrman argued that polite terms such as "pseudepigraphy" hide what was going on. Ancient readers, as Galen and Tertullian show, treated false authorship as deception. A letter that claims to be Paul's and even points to its own signature as proof (2 Thessalonians 3:17) was meant to be believed. By his count several New Testament letters, among them the Pastorals and 2 Peter, are forgeries in that full sense.

Critics push back from two sides. Conservative scholars such as Luke Timothy Johnson defend Paul's authorship of some disputed letters, and others note that Paul wrote with secretaries (Romans 16:22 names one, Tertius) and co-senders, which could explain shifts in style. Other scholars accept that the letters are pseudonymous but reject Ehrman's moral framing. David Meade (1986) argued that writing in an apostle's name could claim his authoritative tradition without lying about who held the pen. Ehrman replies that no ancient source shows such a convention being openly accepted.

concepts.title: Jesus by Letter: Abgar and Lentulus
concepts.contentHtml:
Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Ecclesiastical History (early 4th century), reproduces two letters he says he translated from Syriac records in the archives of Edessa (modern Urfa, in Turkey). King Abgar V of Edessa, who ruled in the early 1st century CE, asks Jesus to come and cure his illness. Jesus replies that he must complete his mission but will send a disciple, and Thaddaeus (Addai in Syriac) duly heals the king. A later Syriac work, the Doctrine of Addai (c. 400 CE), adds that the royal archivist Hannan painted Jesus's portrait, the seed of the legend of the Image of Edessa.

The pilgrim Egeria, visiting Edessa about 384, was told by the bishop that the letter, carried to the city gate, had once turned back a Persian army. Copies were inscribed on stone and worn as amulets. The 6th-century Gelasian Decree classed both letters as apocryphal. Modern scholars treat the exchange as legend, and Walter Bauer (1934) argued it was invented to give one faction in Edessa an apostolic pedigree.

The Letter of Lentulus claims to be a report to the Roman Senate by "Lentulus", an official in Jerusalem, describing Jesus: hair the color of a ripe hazelnut, parted in the middle, a forked beard, blue-gray eyes, a man never known to laugh but often seen to weep. No Roman official of that name and post is known. Scholars date the letter to the later Middle Ages, and it was printed in Ludolph of Saxony's Life of Christ (Cologne, 1474). It describes the bearded, long-haired Jesus of the icons, and its acceptance as an eyewitness report helped fix that image in Western art.

title: The Shapira Scroll
description: A Jerusalem dealer's Deuteronomy, a public unmasking, a suicide, and a scholarly revival 138 years later

concepts.title: Shapira and the Moabite Fakes
concepts.contentHtml:
Moses Wilhelm Shapira was born in 1830 in Kamenets-Podolsk, in the Russian Empire (now Kamianets-Podilskyi, Ukraine), to a Jewish family. On his way to Palestine he converted to Christianity, and by about 1870 he ran a well-known shop for antiquities and manuscripts on Christian Quarter Road in Jerusalem.

His first scandal followed the discovery in 1868 of the Mesha Stele, a 9th-century BCE inscription of the king of Moab that made anything "Moabite" valuable to European museums. In 1873 the Prussian state paid 22,000 thalers for about 1,700 clay figures and vessels, bought through Shapira for the Berlin museum and stamped with letters in Moabite style. The French orientalist Charles Clermont-Ganneau investigated. He traced the "Moabitica" to Salim al-Khouri, a painter and guide who had once made Clermont-Ganneau's own paper squeeze of the Mesha Stele and had since become Shapira's associate, and to craftsmen working with him who copied letters from the stele. Clermont-Ganneau published the objects as forgeries, and the German scholars Emil Kautzsch and Albert Socin came to agree.

Shapira blamed Salim entirely and presented himself as a victim; how much he knew is still debated. His business survived. Through the 1870s he sold genuine Hebrew manuscripts acquired in Yemen to European libraries, including the British Museum. That detail mattered in 1883, because the leather of his next sensation would be compared to those very scrolls.

concepts.title: The Deuteronomy Strips of 1883
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1883 Shapira brought to Europe fifteen leather strips written in the Paleo-Hebrew script, the old alphabet of the Mesha Stele. He said Bedouin had found them in a cave above the Wadi Mujib (the biblical Arnon) east of the Dead Sea, but his accounts of when and how varied. The text was a version of Moses's farewell speeches in Deuteronomy, much shorter than the biblical book and worded differently. Its Ten Commandments came in a different order, with the repeated refrain "I am God, your god", and included an extra commandment: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart."

Shapira asked the British Museum for a million pounds. In August two strips went on public display. But on July 10 a panel in Berlin, including Karl Richard Lepsius and Eduard Sachau, had already examined the strips for about ninety minutes and unanimously called them fakes. In London, Clermont-Ganneau saw the two exhibited strips and declared them forgeries on August 21; the museum's appointed examiner, the Hebraist Christian David Ginsburg, reached the same verdict. Both argued that the leather had been cut from the margins of Yemenite Torah scrolls of the kind Shapira had sold the museum; Ginsburg noted that the writing ignored faint ruling lines on the leather.

Shapira fled London, writing to Ginsburg that he did not think he could survive the shame. On March 9, 1884, he shot himself in a hotel in Rotterdam. The strips were auctioned at Sotheby's in 1885 and bought by the bookseller Bernard Quaritch for £10 5s. They were last shown publicly in 1889 and have since disappeared. Only transcriptions, drawings and newspaper reports survive, so no modern laboratory test is possible.

concepts.title: Dershowitz's Case and the Replies
concepts.contentHtml:
The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls from 1947 onward, in caves by the same sea, made Shapira's story look less absurd. In 1956 Menahem Mansoor of the University of Wisconsin argued that the case deserved re-examination, and a few scholars suggested the strips might be ancient; most, including Moshe Goshen-Gottstein, rejected the idea.

In 2021 Idan Dershowitz, a Bible scholar at the University of Potsdam, went much further in an article and a book, The Valediction of Moses. Working from the 19th-century transcriptions, he argued that the text was not a forger's rewrite of Deuteronomy but an ancient composition from which Deuteronomy grew, which would make it the oldest known biblical manuscript. He added new archival evidence: three overlooked pages in the Berlin State Library preserving Shapira's own preliminary transcription, which he read as Shapira struggling to decipher the text. A forger, he reasoned, would not labor to read his own work. His central argument was literary: the texts' relationship, he said, only makes sense if the Valediction came first.

Most epigraphers and Hebrew linguists were not persuaded. Ronald Hendel and Matthieu Richelle set out "the case for forgery" in Biblical Archaeology Review (Winter 2021), opposite a pro-authenticity article by Dershowitz and James Tabor. The epigrapher Christopher Rollston argued that the case for a 19th-century fake remained strong, and the linguist Benjamin Suchard argued that the text's spelling and grammar depend on the traditional Masoretic text and point to a forger working between about 1870 and 1880. André Lemaire had earlier (1997) found that the letter shapes match no known ancient script. With the leather lost, the dispute can only be argued from copies, and the majority view remains forgery.

title: The Secret Gospel of Mark
description: A letter found at Mar Saba in 1958, pages that later vanished, and more than sixty years of argument

concepts.title: A Letter in the Back of a Book
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1958 Morton Smith, a historian of antiquity at Columbia University, was cataloging manuscripts in the tower library of Mar Saba, a Greek Orthodox monastery in the Judean desert about 20 km southeast of Jerusalem. On the blank endpapers at the back of a printed book, Isaac Vossius's 1646 edition of the letters of Ignatius of Antioch, he found Greek handwriting that paleographers date to the 18th century. It was a copy of a letter attributed to Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 to c. 215 CE) and addressed to an otherwise unknown Theodore.

The letter attacks the Carpocratians, a 2nd-century sect, and says that Mark, after writing his gospel, came to Alexandria and composed "a more spiritual gospel" for those being initiated into the great mysteries. The Carpocratians, Clement says, obtained a copy and corrupted it, so Theodore should deny the secret gospel's existence, even under oath. Clement then quotes two passages. The first, placed after Mark 10:34, has Jesus raise a young man from a tomb in Bethany; six days later the youth comes to him at night "wearing a linen cloth over his naked body", and Jesus teaches him "the mystery of the kingdom of God". The second, after Mark 10:46a, says only that the youth's sister, his mother and Salome were there and Jesus did not receive them. The letter then breaks off mid-sentence.

Smith photographed the pages, announced the find at the Society of Biblical Literature meeting in December 1960, and published it in 1973, in a scholarly edition from Harvard University Press and a popular book, The Secret Gospel.

concepts.title: Smith's Reading and the Vanishing Pages
concepts.contentHtml:
Smith read the fragment as a window on a hidden early Christianity. In his reconstruction Jesus initiated chosen disciples at night, perhaps by a baptismal rite, into the kingdom of God, freeing them from the Mosaic law; his later book Jesus the Magician (1978) cast Jesus as a practitioner of magic. The passage has a naked youth spending the night with Jesus, and Clement insists that the Carpocratian phrase "naked man with naked man" is not in the true text. Smith added, in one speculative sentence, that the spiritual union might have been completed by a physical one. Sexuality has shadowed the debate ever since; Scott Brown later argued that Smith's talk of libertinism meant religious freedom, not sexual license.

In 1976 four scholars from Jerusalem, Guy Stroumsa, David Flusser, Shlomo Pines and Archimandrite Meliton, found the book still at Mar Saba and took it to the library of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate in Jerusalem, a visit Stroumsa made public only in 2003. There the librarian removed the handwritten pages from the book. Color photographs were taken in 1983 and published in 2000 by Charles Hedrick and Nikolaos Olympiou. The pages later went missing, and their whereabouts are unknown.

The ink and paper were never tested. Every argument about Secret Mark therefore rests on photographs, on the Greek of the letter, and on judgments about Smith himself. That is the main reason the question has never been settled.

concepts.title: Hoax, Ancient Letter, or Something Between
concepts.contentHtml:
Quentin Quesnell first raised the possibility of a modern hoax in print in 1975, and Philip Jenkins (2001) noted parallels with The Mystery of Mar Saba (1940), James Hunter's thriller about a forged Christian text found at the monastery. Stephen Carlson's The Gospel Hoax (2005) accused Smith outright of forging the letter and planting clues: a line about salt losing its savor when mixed, which Carlson linked to modern free-flowing table salt and the Morton Salt brand; a hidden signature in another manuscript Smith had photographed; and a "forger's tremor" in the handwriting. Peter Jeffery (2007) argued that the text reflects 20th-century liturgy and sexual attitudes. In 2011 the Greek paleographer Agamemnon Tselikas judged the hand an imitation of 18th-century script.

Defenders answered point by point. Scott Brown's Mark's Other Gospel (2005) argued for authenticity, and Brown and Allan Pantuck disputed Carlson's clues; other researchers found the "tremor" only in printed halftone reproductions, not in the photographs themselves. In 2010 the document examiner Venetia Anastasopoulou concluded that Smith, whose own Greek handwriting was schoolboyish, was very unlikely to have written the letter. Guy Stroumsa, who published Smith's correspondence with Gershom Scholem in 2008, argued that it shows Smith wrestling with the text as a genuine puzzle.

The field remains divided. A third position has gained ground: that the letter is old but not by Clement. Geoffrey Smith and Brent Landau (2023) argue that Morton Smith lacked the skill to forge it and that it is a later pseudepigraph, perhaps written in a monastic setting to defend the rite of brother-making (adelphopoiesis). Many scholars now decline to build arguments about the earliest Christians on it either way.

title: The Gospel of Jesus's Wife
description: A papyrus smaller than a business card, a Harvard announcement, and the reporter who found its owner

concepts.title: "My Wife": The Rome Announcement
concepts.contentHtml:
On September 18, 2012, at the International Congress of Coptic Studies in Rome, Karen L. King, Hollis Professor of Divinity at Harvard Divinity School, presented a papyrus scrap about 4 by 8 cm, smaller than a business card. One side carried eight incomplete lines of Coptic. One line read, "Jesus said to them, 'My wife...'"; others said that "Mary is worthy of it" and that someone "will be able to be my disciple". King proposed that it was a 4th-century copy of a gospel composed in Greek in the 2nd century, and gave it the working title Gospel of Jesus's Wife.

King was careful on one point. She said the fragment did not show that the historical Jesus was married, only that some early Christians discussed the question, in debates about marriage, celibacy and discipleship. But the title traveled faster than the caveat. She also went public before any scientific testing. The owner was anonymous. The provenance offered was a 1999 purchase from a German collector, Hans-Ulrich Laukamp, backed by a typed 1982 letter attributed to the Berlin Egyptologist Peter Munro and a note about the opinion of another Egyptologist, Gerhard Fecht. Laukamp, Munro and Fecht were all dead by 2012, so none could confirm the story.

Doubts surfaced within days. Several Coptic specialists found the handwriting crude and the grammar odd, and the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano dismissed the fragment as a fake. The decisive evidence, though, would come from three directions: the text itself, the laboratory, and the paper trail.

concepts.title: Testing a Text and a Papyrus
concepts.contentHtml:
The first blow was textual. Within weeks Francis Watson of Durham University argued that the fragment was a patchwork of phrases from the Coptic Gospel of Thomas, known from the Nag Hammadi library. Andrew Bernhard then showed that every line could be matched to Michael Grondin's free online interlinear Coptic-English edition of Thomas. A modern forger working from a modern study aid would leave exactly that trace.

In April 2014 the Harvard Theological Review published King's article together with laboratory reports. Radiocarbon dating placed the papyrus in roughly the 7th to 9th centuries CE: centuries later than King's proposed copy, but still old. Raman spectroscopy at Columbia University found a carbon-based ink, a type used in antiquity but also easy to make today. Supporters read the results as consistent with authenticity. Critics replied that nothing in them ruled out a modern hand writing on old blank papyrus, which can be bought on the antiquities market. The same issue carried a rebuttal by Leo Depuydt of Brown University, who called the fragment a forgery.

The owner had also supplied a fragment of the Gospel of John in Lycopolitan, a Coptic dialect, apparently in the same hand and ink. In 2014 Christian Askeland showed that its lines reproduced every second line of a 1924 published edition of an early Lycopolitan codex of John, a text freely available online, and argued that the dialect had probably fallen out of use before the date the tests gave the papyrus. If the John fragment was forged, its twin almost certainly was too.

concepts.title: Ariel Sabar Finds Walter Fritz
concepts.contentHtml:
The paper trail was the last piece. The journalist Ariel Sabar, reporting for The Atlantic, traced the anonymous owner and in June 2016 named him: Walter Fritz, a German-born former Egyptology student at the Free University of Berlin, living in Florida. Fritz first denied owning the papyrus, then admitted it. Sabar found that Laukamp's relatives and associates said he had never owned or shown interest in such papyri, that the Munro letter appeared to be forged, and that Fritz had left his Egyptology studies after a plagiarism accusation.

Fritz denied forging the fragment, while conceding to Sabar that he could have done so had he tried. Within days King said that the new information tipped the balance toward forgery, and she accepted that the papyrus was probably a fake. Sabar's book Veritas (2020) went further, reporting undisclosed conflicts of interest among the scientists consulted and lapses at several stages of the vetting. The Harvard Theological Review did not retract King's article, which still stands as the record of what was claimed and tested in 2014.

The laboratory results were compatible with authenticity but could not prove it. The text betrayed modern copying, and the provenance collapsed once a reporter checked it.

title: The James Ossuary on Trial
description: A bone box naming the brother of Jesus, a forgery trial, an acquittal, and a debate the verdict did not end

concepts.title: James, Son of Joseph, Brother of Jesus
concepts.contentHtml:
Ossuaries are limestone chests in which Jews in and around Jerusalem placed the bones of the dead about a year after burial, once the flesh had decayed, a practice common from roughly the late 1st century BCE until 70 CE. Thousands survive, a minority inscribed with names. On October 21, 2002, at a press conference in Washington, D.C., Hershel Shanks, editor of Biblical Archaeology Review, and the French epigrapher André Lemaire announced one with an Aramaic inscription: Ya'akov bar Yosef akhui di Yeshua, "James son of Joseph brother of Jesus".

If genuine, and if it referred to Jesus of Nazareth, it would be the earliest object naming him. The Gospel of Mark lists a James among Jesus's brothers (Mark 6:3), and the historian Josephus records the execution in 62 CE of "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James". The box belonged to Oded Golan, a Tel Aviv engineer and collector who said he had bought it from an antiquities dealer in the 1970s. It went on show at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto in late 2002, after cracking in transit.

The names themselves were common. James (Jacob), Joseph and Jesus (Yeshua) were all among the most frequent male names of the period, and published estimates of how many men in Jerusalem might fit the description run from about two to about twenty, depending on assumptions. The unusual feature is the mention of a brother, rare on ossuaries; supporters argue that only a notable brother would be named. The box had no known findspot.

concepts.title: The Authority's Verdict and the Court's
concepts.contentHtml:
In June 2003 committees appointed by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) concluded that the ossuary was ancient but its inscription a modern forgery. The geologists Yuval Goren and Avner Ayalon argued that the coating inside the letters was not natural patina: its oxygen isotope ratios did not match patina formed in the Jerusalem area, which pointed to an artificial coating applied to fresh carving. Some scholars, such as Rochelle Altman, took a middle view, accepting the first half of the inscription and judging only "brother of Jesus" a later addition. The same month the IAA declared the Jehoash tablet, another object later tied to Golan, a forgery.

In December 2004 Golan, the antiquities dealer Robert Deutsch and two others were indicted as part of an alleged forgery ring. The trial in the Jerusalem District Court opened in 2005 and ran for nearly seven years, with dozens of experts giving conflicting testimony on patina, script and microbiology. The defense produced a photograph of the ossuary, inscription visible, which it dated to 1976; if that date is right, it is hard to square with a recent forgery.

On March 14, 2012, Judge Aharon Farkash acquitted Golan and Deutsch of all forgery charges. He ruled that the prosecution had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the inscription was forged, and stressed that this was not a finding that it was authentic. Golan was convicted only of lesser offenses related to antiquities dealing, fined 30,000 shekels, and given a one-month sentence he had already served. The state's later effort to keep the objects failed, and they were returned to him.

concepts.title: The Jehoash Tablet and the Limits of Proof
concepts.contentHtml:
The Jehoash tablet is a dark stone slab inscribed with about fifteen lines in the Old Hebrew script, recording repairs to a sacred building in words that closely track 2 Kings 12, the account of King Jehoash of Judah repairing the Temple in the 9th century BCE. It became public in early 2003, said to have been found in a Muslim cemetery near the Temple Mount; police later traced it to Golan, who at first denied owning it. Geologists of the Geological Survey of Israel initially reported a patina containing microscopic gold globules and carbon particles that radiocarbon-dated to antiquity. The IAA committee disagreed: it found spellings and usages that do not fit ancient Hebrew and a mixture of letter forms, and a patina in the letters that differed from the back of the stone and could be rubbed off.

The 2012 verdict treated the tablet like the ossuary: forgery not proven, authenticity not established. Legal proof and scholarly proof differ. A criminal court asks whether forgery was proved beyond reasonable doubt; historians ask which explanation is more probable and avoid resting conclusions on evidence of doubtful origin. Epigraphers such as Lemaire and Ada Yardeni accepted the ossuary inscription, the IAA's experts rejected it, and the geologist Amnon Rosenfeld and colleagues have kept publishing arguments for both objects.

Neither object came from a recorded excavation, so no test can tie either to a tomb or site. A 2007 documentary, The Lost Tomb of Jesus, claimed the ossuary came from a tomb excavated at Talpiot in Jerusalem in 1980; most archaeologists rejected this. Even a wholly ancient inscription would not prove that this James, Joseph and Jesus were the family of the Gospels.

title: Fakes, Loot and the Museum of the Bible
description: Sixteen false scroll fragments, thousands of smuggled tablets, and the tools that catch both

concepts.title: Sixteen Fragments That Were Never at Qumran
concepts.contentHtml:
The Museum of the Bible opened in Washington, D.C., in November 2017, backed by Steve Green, president of the Hobby Lobby craft-store chain, whose family began buying biblical artifacts in 2009. Among its prizes were sixteen small fragments said to come from the Dead Sea Scrolls, bought in four batches between 2009 and 2014. Seven came from William Kando, son of Khalil Iskander Shahin ("Kando"), the Bethlehem dealer who had handled scrolls from the original 1947 finds.

They belonged to a group of about seventy unprovenanced "post-2002" fragments that reached the market from about 2002 onward, bought by collectors and by evangelical institutions such as Azusa Pacific University. From 2016 scholars including Kipp Davis and Årstein Justnes raised doubts: some letters were squeezed into spaces or followed broken edges, as if written on material already damaged. In 2018 the museum sent five fragments to Germany's Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM), which judged them probably forged, and in October the museum took them off display.

In March 2020 a team led by the art-fraud investigator Colette Loll released a report concluding that all sixteen were modern forgeries. At least fifteen were written on leather, not the parchment typical of the scrolls; the leather was probably ancient, perhaps from Roman-era shoes or sandals. The pieces were coated with an amber-colored substance, likely animal-skin glue, to mimic the look of real fragments, and dusted with clay like the sediment of the Qumran caves. Under the microscope the ink pooled in cracks and ran over torn edges: the text went on after the leather was already old and broken. Emanuel Tov noted that the report lacked comparison tests on undisputed scrolls.

concepts.title: Hobby Lobby and the Looted Tablets
concepts.contentHtml:
The forgeries were an embarrassment; the smuggling was a federal case. In December 2010 Hobby Lobby bought thousands of artifacts from Iraq, including cuneiform tablets and clay seal impressions, for about $1.6 million through dealers in the United Arab Emirates and Israel. Two months earlier an expert it had consulted warned that such material might be looted and that improper import could break the law. The shipments arrived in 2011 declared as ceramic or clay tile samples, with false countries of origin, and US customs seized several.

In July 2017 Hobby Lobby settled a civil forfeiture complaint brought by federal prosecutors in Brooklyn: it paid $3 million and forfeited more than 5,500 objects, the first of which were handed back to Iraq in 2018. Steve Green said he had known little about the world of collecting and that the criticism was justified. More cases followed. The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, a cuneiform fragment of the Epic of Gilgamesh that Hobby Lobby bought in 2014 for more than $1.6 million through Christie's, turned out to have a false provenance; it was seized in 2019 and returned to Iraq in 2021. In 2019 the Egypt Exploration Society reported that at least eleven papyrus fragments from its Oxyrhynchus collection at Oxford had been sold to the Greens, sales it linked to the papyrologist Dirk Obbink, who denied the allegations. The museum agreed to return them.

In 2021 the museum returned about 5,000 papyrus fragments to Egypt and some 8,000 clay objects to Iraq. Investigators and journalists describe the case as an example of how wealthy buyers' demand for biblical objects can pull looted material out of war zones.

concepts.title: How Fakes Are Caught
concepts.contentHtml:
Provenance comes first. A genuine object usually has a documented chain: an excavation record, an export permit, or a collection history traceable to before 1970, the year of the UNESCO Convention against illicit trafficking in cultural property, which many museums now use as a cutoff. Every case in this topic failed that test. Shapira's cave story shifted; Secret Mark's original vanished; the Jesus's Wife paperwork named dead men; the ossuary had no findspot; the post-2002 fragments appeared from nowhere. Missing provenance does not prove forgery, but it removes the evidence that could most easily prove authenticity, and buying such objects rewards looting.

Materials science asks what an object is made of and when. Radiocarbon dating measures when the plant or animal behind papyrus, parchment or leather died, not when the ink went on, which is why forgers seek old blank material. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence identify inks and pigments; isotope analysis tests whether a patina formed naturally; microscopy shows whether ink sits over cracks, wear and dirt, which a scribe writing on fresh material could not produce. Each test can expose a fake, but none can prove authenticity; a clean result only means no anachronism was found.

Text and script are the third line. Philologists look for modern spellings, grammar from the wrong period, or copying from a modern edition, as with the Gospel of Jesus's Wife and its twin John fragment. Paleographers judge letter forms, though experts often disagree. The strongest verdicts combine all three: the Jesus's Wife fragment passed its lab tests but failed on text and provenance, while the Museum of the Bible fragments failed under the microscope.
